newsitem.title: UK: UK rules on cloning not enough - ministers.
newsitem.headline: UK rules on cloning not enough - ministers.

text.p: British ministers said on Monday their country's extensive review committees which examine biotechnology and genetic engineering were not enough to ease public fears about cloning.

Thinking ahead and discussing such issues as research on human embryos and transgenic animals had helped Britain become a leader in biotechnology, but more work needed to be done to build public confidence, they told a conference.

"The regulatory system alone cannot carry the burden of maintaining public confidence. All those with an interest in the technology must work closely together to achieve this," Environment Secretary John Gummer told a national biotechnology conference.
Gummer said the public supported biotechnology when it offered clear benefits, such as in the field of medicine, but were sceptical about its wider implications.

News that scientists at Scotland's Roslin Institute had cloned a sheep sent shivers around the world, with U.S. President Bill Clinton calling for the National Biotechnology Advisory Commission to report on the implications, and meantime tightening a ban on federal funding of human clone research.

"I would like to see the industry adopt and develop effective voluntary measures," Gummer told the 200 delegates, who included scientists, experts from environmental and medical bodies and consumer groups.
"The UK is ahead of the world in its arrangements for addressing the ethical issues raised by genetics," Science and Technology Minister Ian Taylor told them.

He said he had written to European Research Commissioner Edith Cresson outlining Britain's regulatory and advisory framework, which includes the Human Genetics Advisory Commission, the Human Fertilisation and Enbryology Authority and the less-official Nuffield Council on Bioethics.
"Our existing framework of advisory and regulatory bodies enables UK scientists to work at the frontiers of knowledge, as with the remarkable breakthrough at the Roslin Institute," Taylor added.

Taylor said he had discussed the possible regulation of genetics with other ministers from the G7 group of industrialised countries, which comprises Britain, Canada, Italy, Germany, the United States, Japan and France.
Trade minister Ian Lang pointed out the business opportunities offered by biotechnology.
"We have a first-class science base capable of delivering this and an industry which leads the way in Europe in industrial exploitation," he said.
"This is important with world markets for biotechnology-derived products forecast to grow rapidly and to pass 70 billion pounds ($110 billion) by the year 2000."
